title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), do there exist constants \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\in (0,1), K_{\varepsilon}>0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair of length-n strings \(x,y, A_{\varepsilon}\) runs in at most \(K_{\varepsilon}(n+2)^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time and outputs an integer D satisfying \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\)? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy \(O(\log  n)\) bits. Use a word RAM with word length \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common positive saving for all \(\varepsilon\), or efficient procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) is required. Rational \(\varepsilon\) suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in \(O(n^{2- \delta})\) time for any fixed \(\delta >0\). A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing \(\varepsilon =0.01\) fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\) must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as \(n^{2}/\log ^{i} n\), for fixed i, is \(n^{2- o(1)}\) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as \(\varepsilon\) approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation for each constant \(\varepsilon\) in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)} n}\) time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed \(\eta >0, a\) constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time. The approximation constant depends on \(\eta\) and is not guaranteed to be \(1+\varepsilon\) for an arbitrarily prescribed \(\varepsilon\). Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before the input length grows; choosing \(\varepsilon\) below \(1/n\) to force exactness is outside any fixed-\(\varepsilon\) runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When \(ED=0 a\) successful estimate must be zero, and when \(ED=1\) and \(\varepsilon <1\) an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.

why: Determine whether arbitrarily accurate fixed-factor approximation can break the quadratic exponent for a central sequence-alignment problem. This tests a different computational boundary from constant-factor estimation with nearly linear overhead.

importance.reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.

progress.text: Backurs–Indyk establish a conditional strongly subquadratic barrier for exact edit distance.
Rubinstein explicitly asks for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in truly subquadratic time as Open question 2.
Andoni–Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for each fixed \(\eta >0\); the approximation constant is not arbitrarily close to one.
Mao–Rubinstein give a randomized near-exact approximation scheme with a quasipolynomial improvement over quadratic time, accepted to STOC 2026.

status_note: No resolution with a fixed positive exponent saving for every fixed \(\varepsilon\) was found in the primary-source check through 11 September 2026. The 2026 scheme improves quadratic time by a quasipolynomial factor and does not establish the target \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) bound.
review_note: Added on the user’s explicit request to retain both edit-distance variants. The original question, the 2026 introduction and Theorem 6.1, and the primary constant-factor and exact-hardness statements were checked. The word-RAM and worst-case randomized conventions are editorial clarifications matching TCS-6624. The status review does not independently verify the proofs of the cited papers.

sentences: Unit-cost edit distance counts the fewest single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another.

The question asks whether every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) permits a randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) time for some fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\) on every input pair.
Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 approximation scheme gives a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time without establishing that fixed exponent saving.
The numerical estimate must have purely multiplicative error even for strings with very small distance, and all preprocessing is included in the runtime.
This accuracy target remains separate from TCS-6624, which allows a fixed constant factor but requires \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time.
